publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Global prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders in 204 countries and territories in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the change in prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders in 2020 across 204 countries and territories, estimated for locations with and without data
span.quote: In this study, we aimed to quantify the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders globally in 2020.

span.label: how much did the COVID-19 pandemic raise the global prevalence and burden of depression and anxiety, by age, sex and location
span.quote: In this study, we aimed to quantify the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the prevalence and burden of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders globally in 2020.

span.label: the first global estimate of the pandemic's effect on these two disorders, and a data standard the authors offer to the field for measuring the next population shock
span.quote: This study is the first to quantify the prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders by age, sex, and location globally.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We estimated an additional 53·2 million (44·8 to 62·9) cases of major depressive disorder globally (an increase of 27·6% \[25·1 to 30·3\]) due to the COVID-19 pandemic, such that the total prevalence was 3152·9 cases (2722·5 to 3654·5) per 100 000 population.

span.label: a population shock raising the prevalence of common mental disorders - the same pattern seen after the 2008 and 2009 financial crises, now measured globally
span.quote: Our study is not the first to show how population shocks (ie, unexpected or unpredictable events that disrupt the environmental, health, economic, or social circumstances within a population) can increase the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. In their review of mental health outcomes after the economic crisis in 2009, Frasquilho and colleagues 24 identified several studies showing an increase in common mental disorders in the general population.

span.label: systematic review restricted to surveys with a pre-pandemic baseline, then Bayesian meta-regression (MR-BRT) of the prevalence change against COVID-19 impact indicators, applied to DisMod-MR 2.1 pre-pandemic estimates for every GBD location
span.term: systematic review restricted to surveys with a pre-pandemic baseline, then Bayesian meta-regression (MR-BRT) of the prevalence change against COVID-19 impact indicators, applied to DisMod-MR 2.1 pre-pandemic estimates for every GBD location
span.quote: First, we conducted a systematic literature review to assemble data from surveys measuring the effect of COVID-19 on the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. Second, we used these data in a meta-analysis to (1) estimate the change in prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders before versus during the COVID-19 pandemic, (2) predict (through the use of selected indicators of COVID-19 impact) the resulting change in prevalence of each disorder across all GBD locations, and (3) translate changes in prevalence to corresponding changes in burden estimates as years lived with disability (YLDs) and DALYs.

span.label: why women were affected more: carer and household load from school closures, lower salaries and less secure employment, and a measured rise in domestic violence during lockdowns - social channels rather than biological ones
span.quote: Additional carer and household responsibilities due to school closures or family members becoming unwell are more likely to fall on women. Women are more likely to be financially disadvantaged during the pandemic due to lower salaries, less savings, and less secure employment than their male counterparts. 17, 18, 19 They are also more likely to be victims of domestic violence, the prevalence of which increased during periods of lockdown and stay-at-home orders.

span.label: why the young were affected more: 1.6 billion learners out of school in over 190 countries, no physical spaces for peer interaction, and a higher chance of unemployment during and after an economic crisis
span.quote: UNESCO declared COVID-19 to be the most severe disruption to global education in history, estimating 1·6 billion learners in over 190 countries to be fully or partially out of school in 2020. With school closures and wider social restrictions in place, young people have been unable to come together in physical spaces, affecting their ability to learn and for peer interaction. Furthermore, young people are more likely to become unemployed during and following economic crises than older people.

span.label: the general category the paper places COVID-19 in - an unexpected event disrupting a population's environmental, health, economic or social circumstances, with the 2008-09 financial crises as its worked precedents
span.quote: Our study is not the first to show how population shocks (ie, unexpected or unpredictable events that disrupt the environmental, health, economic, or social circumstances within a population) can increase the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. In their review of mental health outcomes after the economic crisis in 2009, Frasquilho and colleagues 24 identified several studies showing an increase in common mental disorders in the general population.

span.label: distancing and travel restriction made medication and in-person care harder to get, services were interrupted or redirected, and people avoided seeking care for fear of infection - demand up and supply down together
span.term: care interrupted at the moment of need
span.quote: Perhaps more importantly, no reduction in the global prevalence or burden was detected for either disorder since 1990, despite compelling evidence of interventions that reduce their impact.

span.label: the two indicators are unlikely to have captured the full impact of the pandemic, and infection rates are not consistently measured or reported everywhere
span.quote: First, we were limited by the data available to consistently measure the effect of COVID-19 across all GBD locations using our choice of COVID-19 indicators. Human mobility and SARS-CoV-2 infection rates are unlikely to have captured the full impact of the pandemic on mental health across all countries.

span.label: mobile-phone mobility tracking is inaccurate where phone use is low, and people who cannot reduce their mobility because of their job may have their mobility drop overestimated - a bias with a direction, stated
span.quote: Reliance on mobile phone tracking technology to monitor human mobility will also not be accurate in locations where subgroups of the population (eg, people of low socioeconomic status) have little or no mobile phone use. Some subgroups might not be able to reduce their mobility because of their employment type and might be more prone to infection, and so reductions in human mobility might be exaggerated in these locations.

span.label: VERY FEW QUALIFYING SURVEYS FROM LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES, and large increases were nonetheless estimated for Latin America and the Caribbean, north Africa and the Middle East, and south Asia - super-regions from which NO study met the inclusion criteria at all
span.quote: Second, we found very few surveys that met our inclusion criteria from low-income and middle-income countries, meaning that findings from our regression analysis might be less generalisable to these locations. For example, we estimated large increases in prevalence within Latin America and the Caribbean, north Africa and the Middle East, and south Asia, despite not finding any surveys from these super-regions that met our inclusion criteria.

span.label: so the paper asks readers not to extrapolate rankings between countries, and its own leave-one-country-out cross-validation showed the rankings move with data availability
span.quote: Our leave-one-country-out cross-validation analysis showed that although our estimates are generally within the bounds of uncertainty for re-predicting data for missing locations, the relative rankings of locations were affected by data availability.

span.label: most surveys used symptom scales estimating PROBABLE cases; the assumption that screening thresholds kept their predictive validity through the pandemic could bias the estimates, and a high anxiety score in 2020 might be a natural reaction to a real threat
span.quote: However, this assumption has the potential to bias our estimates. For example, high scores on anxiety disorder symptom scales might reflect a natural psychological and physiological reaction to a perceived threat (ie, the COVID-19 pandemic) rather than a probable anxiety disorder.

span.label: only three diagnostic surveys existed to test that assumption against; two showed increases and the third used very small samples and changed from face-to-face to telephone administration at the pandemic's onset
span.quote: We identified only three diagnostic mental health surveys that had been done since the beginning of the pandemic. Increases in prevalence were observed in two of the three diagnostic surveys. 39, 40 The study that did not report an increased prevalence was conducted in one specific city in Norway (Trondheim) using very small cross-sectional samples. The authors of this study also reported that the shift from face-to-face to telephone survey administration occurred at the onset of the pandemic, which might have affected interviewers' ability to identify mental disorders, especially in the early stages of this shift when they were less experienced with telephone survey administration.

span.label: the severity distribution had to be assumed unchanged - existing cases may have worsened and new cases may be milder, and the burden estimate cannot tell
span.quote: The paucity of diagnostic surveys conducted during the pandemic also meant that we were unable to explore its effect on the severity distribution of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. We estimated prevalent cases of each disorder but could not assess how existing cases changed in their severity. Existing cases might have worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic, while novel cases might have had milder disorder severity. For the burden analysis presented, we had to assume that the severity distribution of both existing and new cases remained unchanged from before the COVID-19 pandemic.

span.label: studies were excluded for convenience sampling, non-standard case definitions, and instruments with no comparable pre-pandemic estimate
span.quote: Fourth, many studies needed to be excluded from our systematic review because of reliance on convenience sampling strategies (eg, snowball sampling), case definitions that did not adhere to internationally accepted definitions for mental disorders, and use of survey instruments for which no comparable pre-pandemic estimate was available.

span.label: other disorders may also have been affected - eating disorders are named - and were not estimated because the data have not been assessed
span.quote: Fifth, prevalences of mental disorders other than major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders might have also been affected by COVID-19. For instance, emerging evidence suggests that other disorders such as eating disorders have been affected by the COVID-19 pandemic but these data have yet to be appropriately assessed.

span.label: whether the increased prevalence came with increased suicide is left open: a 21-country time-series found no significant rise, and the authors say they have insufficient data to conclude either way
span.quote: In their time-series analysis of the impact of COVID-19 on suicide rates across 21 high-income and middle-income countries, Pirkis and colleagues 30 found no significant increases in suicide rates between April and July, 2020. This finding raises the question of whether or not the increased prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders we found was accompanied by a significant increase in suicide rates. We have insufficient data to draw any conclusions on this matter.

span.label: DALYs here are entirely years lived with disability - despite potential excess deaths, neither disorder is counted as an underlying cause of death, which is an ICD convention and not a finding about lethality
span.quote: DALYs for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were composed entirely of YLDs, which meant that, despite potential excess deaths, major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were not considered underlying causes of death.

span.label: the geographical spread of the evidence: 22 studies from western Europe, 14 from high-income North America, 5 Australasia, 5 high-income Asia Pacific, 2 east Asia, 1 central Europe
span.quote: Most studies were from western Europe (n=22) and high-income North America (n=14), and the remaining studies were from Australasia (n=5), high-income Asia Pacific (n=5), east Asia (n=2), and central Europe (n=1; appendix p 20).

span.label: an eligibility rule requiring a comparable PRE-PANDEMIC BASELINE, applied before any modelling: 5,683 sources found, 1,674 past title and abstract, 48 admitted
span.note: eliminates: a during-pandemic prevalence being read as a CHANGE in prevalence. Without a baseline a survey measures a level, and the level was already high - this paper's own introduction notes no reduction since 1990 · outcome: held
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: GBD case definitions tied to DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 rather than to whatever each survey called a case
span.note: eliminates: the pooled estimate being an average over incompatible definitions of depression and anxiety · outcome: held
span.quote: To ensure comparability in measurement, we used case definitions for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders used within the GBD framework. These definitions adhere to criteria presented in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder fourth edition text revision (DSM-IV-TR) 7 and the tenth International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10).

span.label: market-research quota sampling admitted but carried as a bias covariate rather than pooled with random samples
span.note: eliminates: a non-probabilistic sampling frame inflating the estimate silently - AND THE COVARIATE EARNED ITS PLACE: cross-sectional quota studies significantly over-estimated the increase, which the model could then correct for · outcome: held
span.quote: Studies using market research quota sampling were also included but were controlled for with a covariate in our analysis. Market research quota sampling is a non-probabilistic sampling strategy whereby participants are identified from a database to match the population of interest (a discussion of the use of these estimates is in the [appendix \[p 7\]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8500697/#sec1)). Samples obtained via this method might produce results that differ from the general population.

span.label: a separate bias covariate for instruments measuring depression and anxiety symptoms together, such as the K-6
span.note: eliminates: a combined-symptom instrument being counted as evidence about either disorder alone - and again it was measured, not assumed: those instruments overestimated the anxiety increase but not the depression increase · outcome: held
span.quote: Briefly, potential bias covariates that were identified were cross-sectional comparisons informed by random samples, longitudinal comparisons informed by market research and quota samples, cross-sectional comparisons informed by market research and quota samples, and estimates representing combined symptoms of depressive and anxiety disorders

span.label: leave-one-country-out cross-validation of the final model
span.note: eliminates: the estimates for locations with no data being untested - PARTIAL, and the authors report what it found against them: estimates stayed within their uncertainty bounds but the RANKINGS between locations moved with data availability · outcome: partial
span.quote: Our leave-one-country-out cross-validation analysis showed that although our estimates are generally within the bounds of uncertainty for re-predicting data for missing locations, the relative rankings of locations were affected by data availability.

span.label: backward elimination on the Akaike information criterion, with each unique sample given a random intercept and random effects on the impact indicators
span.note: eliminates: covariates surviving in the model on the analyst's preference rather than on fit · outcome: held
span.quote: In step two, we developed a final model for each disorder via backward elimination to regress the COVID-19 impact indicator, age, sex, and the bias covariates on the change in logit prevalence. The least significant covariate was iteratively removed until no improvement was seen in the Akaike information criterion.

span.label: PRISMA reporting, a protocol registered with PROSPERO before the review, and GATHER compliance with all analysis code published
span.note: eliminates: the search and the inclusion rule being decided after the data were seen - the protocol is registered and the code is inspectable · outcome: held
span.quote: We used the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines; 9 our PRISMA checklist is in the appendix (pp 28–31), and the search protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, CRD42021216590).

span.label: no language restriction on the literature search
span.note: eliminates: an English-only search compounding the geographical gap the authors already report - though it did not close it: no qualifying study came from a low- or middle-income country · outcome: partial
span.quote: No language restrictions were applied.

span.label: confirming that no 2020 epidemiological data entered the DisMod-MR model, so its 2020 output is a genuine counterfactual
span.note: eliminates: the pandemic's effect being partly inside the baseline it is measured against - the pre-pandemic prevalence for 2020 is uncontaminated by 2020 · outcome: held
span.quote: Because no epidemiological data from the year 2020 informed the DisMod-MR 2.1 model for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, the prevalence produced for 2020 by age and sex and for each of the 204 countries and territories represented the prevalence of each disorder without the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

span.label: a statement that the funders had no role in design, collection, analysis or interpretation
span.note: eliminates: a funder's interest shaping a global prevalence estimate that policy is set from · outcome: held
span.quote: The funders of the study had no role in the study design

span.label: major depressive disorder
span.quote: We estimated an additional 53·2 million (44·8 to 62·9) cases of major depressive disorder globally (an increase of 27·6% \[25·1 to 30·3\]) due to the COVID-19 pandemic, such that the total prevalence was 3152·9 cases (2722·5 to 3654·5) per 100 000 population.

span.label: anxiety disorders
span.quote: We also estimated an additional 76·2 million (64·3 to 90·6) cases of anxiety disorders globally (an increase of 25·6% \[23·2 to 28·0\]), such that the total prevalence was 4802·4 cases (4108·2 to 5588·6) per 100 000 population.

span.label: prevalence
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: pre-pandemic baseline
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: human mobility
span.quote: After controlling for human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, daily excess mortality rate was not associated with the change in prevalence for either major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. This was likely due to high collinearity between the daily excess mortality rate and the other two COVID-19 impact variables ( _r_ = 0·8 with daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and _r_ = 0·8 with human mobility), which was less of an issue shared between the daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and human mobility

span.label: daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate
span.quote: After controlling for human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, daily excess mortality rate was not associated with the change in prevalence for either major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. This was likely due to high collinearity between the daily excess mortality rate and the other two COVID-19 impact variables ( _r_ = 0·8 with daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and _r_ = 0·8 with human mobility), which was less of an issue shared between the daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and human mobility

span.label: daily excess mortality rate
span.quote: After controlling for human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, daily excess mortality rate was not associated with the change in prevalence for either major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. This was likely due to high collinearity between the daily excess mortality rate and the other two COVID-19 impact variables ( _r_ = 0·8 with daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and _r_ = 0·8 with human mobility), which was less of an issue shared between the daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and human mobility

span.label: COVID-19 pandemic
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: risk factors
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: proxies
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: DisMod-MR 2.1
span.quote: Because no epidemiological data from the year 2020 informed the DisMod-MR 2.1 model for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, the prevalence produced for 2020 by age and sex and for each of the 204 countries and territories represented the prevalence of each disorder without the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

span.label: DALYs
span.quote: DALYs for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were composed entirely of YLDs, which meant that, despite potential excess deaths, major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were not considered underlying causes of death.

span.label: YLDs
span.quote: DALYs for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were composed entirely of YLDs, which meant that, despite potential excess deaths, major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were not considered underlying causes of death.

span.label: market research quota sampling
span.quote: Given the paucity of studies using random sampling of the general population, we took advantage of studies using market research and quota sampling during the COVID-19 pandemic. We found that cross-sectional (but not longitudinal) studies that used market research quota sampling significantly over-estimated the increase in disorder prevalence.

span.label: population shocks
span.quote: Our study is not the first to show how population shocks (ie, unexpected or unpredictable events that disrupt the environmental, health, economic, or social circumstances within a population) can increase the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. In their review of mental health outcomes after the economic crisis in 2009, Frasquilho and colleagues 24 identified several studies showing an increase in common mental disorders in the general population.

span.label: screening measures
span.quote: Studies reporting probable cases of depressive or anxiety disorders using established screening measures were included due to the paucity of available survey data from during the COVID-19 pandemic using diagnostic instruments. In these instances, only prevalence estimates for cases that reached established thresholds for probable depressive or anxiety disorder were included.

span.label: daily excess mortality rate → daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate
span.note: COLLINEAR AT r=0.8, WHICH IS WHY ONE OF THEM IS NOT IN THE MODEL. Excess mortality showed no independent association with the prevalence change once the other two indicators were controlled for, and the paper attributes that to collinearity rather than to absence of effect. None of the eight types says `correlates with`, and none of them can say `dropped from the model because it duplicates another variable` - which is the actual relation and the reason the coefficient is missing
span.quote: After controlling for human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, daily excess mortality rate was not associated with the change in prevalence for either major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. This was likely due to high collinearity between the daily excess mortality rate and the other two COVID-19 impact variables ( _r_ = 0·8 with daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and _r_ = 0·8 with human mobility), which was less of an issue shared between the daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and human mobility

span.label: pre-pandemic baseline → prevalence
span.note: A CRITERION THAT DECIDES WHAT COUNTS AS EVIDENCE. Requiring a comparable pre-pandemic measurement took 5,683 sources to 48 - it is the single most consequential step in the analysis and it is not a relation between two concepts in any of the eight senses. `part-of` is false, `causes` is false, and `operationalised-as` inverts it: the baseline is not how prevalence is measured, it is what makes a measurement admissible
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: COVID-19 impact indicator - THE PAPER PRE-EMPTS ITS OWN MISREADING AND SAYS SO OUTRIGHT: human mobility and infection rate `should not be interpreted as risk factors`. They are PROXIES for the pandemic, which is the risk factor. A reader who takes the coefficient on human mobility as an effect of mobility has read the model backwards, and the authors put the warning in the discussion rather than leaving it to be inferred
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: prevalence, in this paper - A MODELLED QUANTITY, NOT A MEASURED ONE, and for most of the 204 locations there is no survey behind it. DisMod-MR estimates prevalence for locations missing raw data by cascading priors down a five-level geographical hierarchy, so a country's figure can be entirely inherited from its region
span.quote: It also estimates prevalence for locations that are missing raw epidemiological data. GBD 2020 does this by estimating prevalence across a cascade down five levels of a geographical hierarchy: global, super-region, region, country or territory, and subnational locations. The prevalence from locations higher in the hierarchy act as priors for the prevalence for locations lower in the hierarchy.

span.label: case, as counted here - A PROBABLE CASE ON A SCREENING SCALE, not a diagnosis. Only three diagnostic surveys existed to check against. The authors assume the predictive validity of screening thresholds did not change during the pandemic, and then give the counter-example themselves: a high anxiety-scale score in 2020 might be a natural reaction to a real threat rather than a disorder. SAME THRESHOLD PROBLEM AS lai2020, one level up
span.quote: We assumed the predictive validity between probable versus diagnosed cases using these screening measures did not change during the COVID-19 pandemic compared with before the pandemic, and therefore the change in the prevalence of probable cases would be equivalent to the change in the prevalence of diagnosed cases

span.label: pre-pandemic baseline - THE ELIGIBILITY CRITERION, AND THE ONE THAT DID THE WORK. A prevalence survey run during the pandemic was not admissible without comparable data from before it, however large or well conducted. 5,683 sources became 48. Both COVID-19 mental health papers in this corpus - wang2020 and lai2020 - are cross-sectional with no pre-pandemic measurement and would fail it
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: not associated, said of daily excess mortality - A COLLINEARITY RESULT, NOT A NULL EFFECT. Excess mortality correlates at r=0.8 with both surviving indicators, so it drops out of the model after they are controlled for. The paper says the reason. Reading it as `deaths did not affect mental health` is the opposite of what the analysis supports
span.quote: After controlling for human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, daily excess mortality rate was not associated with the change in prevalence for either major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. This was likely due to high collinearity between the daily excess mortality rate and the other two COVID-19 impact variables ( _r_ = 0·8 with daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and _r_ = 0·8 with human mobility), which was less of an issue shared between the daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and human mobility

span.label: claim_type: existence
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: existence — A BLIND second reading by terminal-a on 2026-08-25: the record's own claim_type/method/phenomenon were not looked at until every value here was written and substring-verified. Not applied - a person decides. Sampling frame: the 504 staged records carrying no `alternatives` block, so this never re-measures the 202. All 11 records with 130+ tags were taken as a census and 19 more spread one per discipline across 22 disciplines - the dense non-neuroscience cell is the one the 202 do not contain (inside them, 94-100% of the densest bands are neuroscience; among these 11, one is). See Q-1176, Q-1178.

span.quote: Before 2020, mental disorders were leading causes of the global health-related burden, with depressive and anxiety disorders being leading contributors to this burden.

span.label: critiques → the body of single-location snapshot surveys of depression and anxiety during COVID-19, and the qualitative syntheses and pooled estimates built on them
span.note: the criticism is not of any one survey but of what the set of them cannot do: no study had synthesised a global prevalence and burden for 2020, and the pooled estimates on offer did not adjust for the baseline problem
span.quote: Most of the identified work consisted of surveys done for a specific location, at a snapshot in time, and indicated an increase in prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic. We also found several systematic reviews and meta-analyses to summarise these studies; however, these studies were either qualitative syntheses or simply presented pooled estimates across studies. We did not find any studies that attempted to synthesise the global prevalence and burden of depressive and anxiety disorders due to the COVID-19 pandemic for the year 2020.

span.label: distinguishes-from → surveys of prevalence during the pandemic that lack a comparable pre-pandemic baseline - which is the design of both wang2020 and lai2020 in this corpus
span.note: THE PAPER DOES NOT NAME THOSE TWO. What it states is the criterion, and the criterion excludes their design - both are cross-sectional with no pre-pandemic measurement, and lai2020 says so itself. The relation is to the DESIGN CLASS, not to the papers
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: qualifies → Pirkis and colleagues' 21-country time-series finding no significant increase in suicide rates between April and July 2020
span.note: and the qualification runs BOTH ways - the authors say they have insufficient data to conclude anything, and offer that the window may have been too early rather than claiming the finding is wrong
span.quote: In their time-series analysis of the impact of COVID-19 on suicide rates across 21 high-income and middle-income countries, Pirkis and colleagues 30 found no significant increases in suicide rates between April and July, 2020. This finding raises the question of whether or not the increased prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders we found was accompanied by a significant increase in suicide rates. We have insufficient data to draw any conclusions on this matter.

span.label: builds-on → Frasquilho and colleagues' review of mental health outcomes after the 2009 economic crisis, and the Greek and Hong Kong prevalence series that followed the 2008-09 crashes
span.quote: Our study is not the first to show how population shocks (ie, unexpected or unpredictable events that disrupt the environmental, health, economic, or social circumstances within a population) can increase the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. In their review of mental health outcomes after the economic crisis in 2009, Frasquilho and colleagues 24 identified several studies showing an increase in common mental disorders in the general population.

span.label: extends → GBD 2019's estimates of depressive and anxiety disorder burden, which this study adjusts rather than replaces
span.quote: Because no epidemiological data from the year 2020 informed the DisMod-MR 2.1 model for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders, the prevalence produced for 2020 by age and sex and for each of the 204 countries and territories represented the prevalence of each disorder without the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

span.label: predicts → future mental health surveys responding to COVID-19 or another population shock, which the authors ask to align their sampling and instruments with pre-pandemic baselines
span.note: an unusual relation to record and worth having: the paper is addressing studies that do not exist yet, and the data standard is offered as its second contribution
span.quote: Researchers planning surveys during the pandemic should strive to align their sample representation and measures of mental health with existing pre-pandemic baseline estimates to ensure appropriate comparable data from before and during the pandemic.

span.label: COVID-19 pandemic —causes→ major depressive disorder
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9 — the paper is explicit that the PANDEMIC is the risk factor and the indicators are proxies for it, so this edge and not an indicator edge is the one it licenses
span.quote: We estimated an additional 53·2 million (44·8 to 62·9) cases of major depressive disorder globally (an increase of 27·6% \[25·1 to 30·3\]) due to the COVID-19 pandemic, such that the total prevalence was 3152·9 cases (2722·5 to 3654·5) per 100 000 population.

span.label: COVID-19 pandemic —causes→ anxiety disorders
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: We also estimated an additional 76·2 million (64·3 to 90·6) cases of anxiety disorders globally (an increase of 25·6% \[23·2 to 28·0\]), such that the total prevalence was 4802·4 cases (4108·2 to 5588·6) per 100 000 population.

span.label: COVID-19 pandemic —operationalised-as→ human mobility
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — re-pointed in the audit. It read `human mobility --operationalised-as--> proxies`, and `proxies` is too general an endpoint to be wrong. What the paper says is that these indicators stand in for THE PANDEMIC, so the pandemic is the concept and mobility is how it was measured - the same shape as `psychological impact --operationalised-as--> IES-R` in wang2020
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: COVID-19 pandemic —operationalised-as→ daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: risk factors —distinct-from→ proxies
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — the distinction the paper draws about its own model, in its own discussion, before anyone could get it wrong
span.quote: The two COVID-19 impact indicators used in our model should not be interpreted as risk factors for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders. The risk factor of interest was the COVID-19 pandemic, with these two indicators acting as proxies for the effect of COVID-19 in the population.

span.label: prevalence —operationalised-as→ DisMod-MR 2.1
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — and for locations with no raw data the operationalisation is the whole of it - the figure is a cascaded prior, not a measurement
span.quote: It also estimates prevalence for locations that are missing raw epidemiological data. GBD 2020 does this by estimating prevalence across a cascade down five levels of a geographical hierarchy: global, super-region, region, country or territory, and subnational locations. The prevalence from locations higher in the hierarchy act as priors for the prevalence for locations lower in the hierarchy.

span.label: YLDs —part-of→ DALYs
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — AUDIT REVERSED THIS. Years lived with disability are a COMPONENT of disability-adjusted life-years, not the container. I had written it backwards and then written a note explaining why backwards was acceptable. For these two disorders the component is the whole - DALYs are composed entirely of YLDs, because neither is counted as an underlying cause of death - and that is what makes the containment total here rather than partial
span.quote: DALYs for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were composed entirely of YLDs, which meant that, despite potential excess deaths, major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders were not considered underlying causes of death.

span.label: market research quota sampling —causes→ prevalence
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — a bias with a measured direction, and the qualifier is load-bearing: cross-sectional quota studies overestimated, longitudinal ones did not
span.quote: Given the paucity of studies using random sampling of the general population, we took advantage of studies using market research and quota sampling during the COVID-19 pandemic. We found that cross-sectional (but not longitudinal) studies that used market research quota sampling significantly over-estimated the increase in disorder prevalence.

span.label: population shocks —causes→ major depressive disorder
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85
span.quote: For instance, emerging evidence suggests that other disorders such as eating disorders have been affected by the COVID-19 pandemic but these data have yet to be appropriately assessed. Most of the available scientific literature focuses on changes in symptoms of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorder as a result of COVID-19 because these are historically more sensitive to population shocks.

span.label: an additional 53.2 million cases of major depressive disorder globally in 2020, an increase of 27.6%
span.quote: We estimated an additional 53·2 million (44·8 to 62·9) cases of major depressive disorder globally (an increase of 27·6% \[25·1 to 30·3\]) due to the COVID-19 pandemic, such that the total prevalence was 3152·9 cases (2722·5 to 3654·5) per 100 000 population.

span.label: an additional 76.2 million cases of anxiety disorders, an increase of 25.6%
span.quote: We also estimated an additional 76·2 million (64·3 to 90·6) cases of anxiety disorders globally (an increase of 25·6% \[23·2 to 28·0\]), such that the total prevalence was 4802·4 cases (4108·2 to 5588·6) per 100 000 population.

span.label: 49.4 million DALYs from major depressive disorder and 44.5 million from anxiety disorders in 2020
span.quote: Altogether, major depressive disorder caused 49·4 million (33·6 to 68·7) DALYs and anxiety disorders caused 44·5 million (30·2 to 62·5) DALYs globally in 2020.

span.label: females were affected more than males and younger age groups more than older ones
span.quote: Females were affected more by the pandemic than males ( _B_ 0·1 \[0·1 to 0·2; p=0·0001\] for major depressive disorder, 0·1 \[0·1 to 0·2; p=0·0001\] for anxiety disorders) and younger age groups were more affected than older age groups (−0·007 \[–0·009 to −0·006; p=0·0001\] for major depressive disorder, −0·003 \[–0·005 to −0·002; p=0·0001\] for anxiety disorders).

span.label: the locations hit hardest by the pandemic had the greatest increases
span.quote: We estimated that the locations hit hardest by the pandemic in 2020, as measured with decreased human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, had the greatest increases in prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders.

span.label: 48 of 5,683 identified sources met the inclusion criteria - 46 for depression, 27 for anxiety
span.quote: Of the 5683 unique data sources obtained from the systematic review, 1674 remained following title and abstract screening. In total, 46 studies met inclusion criteria for major depressive disorder and 27 for anxiety disorders (48 in total, one of which reported data across two regions

span.label: AND THE INCREASE WAS ESTIMATED FOR SUPER-REGIONS WITH NO QUALIFYING SURVEY AT ALL - Latin America and the Caribbean, north Africa and the Middle East, south Asia
span.quote: Second, we found very few surveys that met our inclusion criteria from low-income and middle-income countries, meaning that findings from our regression analysis might be less generalisable to these locations. For example, we estimated large increases in prevalence within Latin America and the Caribbean, north Africa and the Middle East, and south Asia, despite not finding any surveys from these super-regions that met our inclusion criteria.

span.label: no reduction in global prevalence or burden of either disorder had been detected since 1990, before the pandemic began
span.quote: Perhaps more importantly, no reduction in the global prevalence or burden was detected for either disorder since 1990, despite compelling evidence of interventions that reduce their impact.

span.label: eligible study = reported prevalence during the pandemic AND had a comparable pre-pandemic baseline; without one it could not be included
span.quote: Eligible studies reported prevalence of depressive or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic and had a pre-pandemic baseline. We used timelines for these periods as defined by each study. Prevalence surveys conducted during the pandemic could not be included without comparable pre-pandemic data

span.label: COVID-19 impact indicator = something that captures an effect of COVID-19, is consistently measured across locations, and is measured with sufficient granularity over time
span.quote: A COVID-19 impact indicator had to capture an effect of COVID-19, be consistently measured across locations, and be consistently measured with sufficient granularity across time (preferably daily or weekly) over the course of the pandemic.

span.label: population shock = an unexpected or unpredictable event disrupting the environmental, health, economic or social circumstances of a population
span.quote: Our study is not the first to show how population shocks (ie, unexpected or unpredictable events that disrupt the environmental, health, economic, or social circumstances within a population) can increase the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. In their review of mental health outcomes after the economic crisis in 2009, Frasquilho and colleagues 24 identified several studies showing an increase in common mental disorders in the general population.

span.label: case definitions taken from the GBD framework, adhering to DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10
span.quote: To ensure comparability in measurement, we used case definitions for major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders used within the GBD framework. These definitions adhere to criteria presented in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorder fourth edition text revision (DSM-IV-TR) 7 and the tenth International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10).

span.label: the three candidate indicators: decreasing human mobility, estimated TOTAL rather than reported daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, and estimated daily excess mortality including deaths not attributed to COVID-19
span.quote: Ultimately, we considered three novel indicators of the COVID-19 pandemic: decreasing human mobility, 13 estimated total (as opposed to reported) daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, and estimated daily excess mortality rate during the pandemic (including excess deaths occurring during the pandemic where COVID-19 was not reported as the underlying cause of death

span.label: excess mortality correlates at r=0.8 with both surviving indicators and at 0.5 between them, which is why it drops from the model rather than because it has no effect
span.quote: After controlling for human mobility and daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate, daily excess mortality rate was not associated with the change in prevalence for either major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders. This was likely due to high collinearity between the daily excess mortality rate and the other two COVID-19 impact variables ( _r_ = 0·8 with daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and _r_ = 0·8 with human mobility), which was less of an issue shared between the daily SARS-CoV-2 infection rate and human mobility

span.label: cross-sectional market-research quota studies significantly over-estimated the prevalence increase; longitudinal ones using the same sampling did not
span.quote: Given the paucity of studies using random sampling of the general population, we took advantage of studies using market research and quota sampling during the COVID-19 pandemic. We found that cross-sectional (but not longitudinal) studies that used market research quota sampling significantly over-estimated the increase in disorder prevalence.

span.label: instruments combining depression and anxiety symptoms overestimated the anxiety increase but not the depression increase
span.quote: We also found instruments that captured symptoms of both depressive and anxiety disorders combined overestimated the increase in prevalence of anxiety disorders, but not major depressive disorder. This could be because they captured more new depressive disorder cases than anxiety disorder cases.

span.label: 95% uncertainty intervals are the 25th and 975th of 1,000 posterior samples
span.quote: We report estimates with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs), which represent the 25th and 975th ranked results across the 1000 samples and can be interpreted similarly to 95% CIs.

span.label: after the 2009 Greek crisis, point prevalence of major depressive episodes went from 3.3% in 2008 to 6.8% in 2009 to 8.2% in 2011
span.quote: After the 2009 financial crisis in Greece, point prevalence of major depressive episodes increased from 3·3% (95% UI 3·1–3·5) in 2008 to 6·8% (6·4–7·2) in 2009 and 8·2% (8·1–8·3) in 2011. Survey respondents reporting serious economic hardship were most at risk of developing a major depressive episode.

span.label: in Japan suicide fell 14% over the first five pandemic months and then rose 16%, more among females and the young
span.quote: For example, Tanaka and Okamota 31 found that, although suicide rates in Japan decreased by 14% during the first 5 months of the pandemic (February to June, 2020), they then increased by 16% (between July and October, 2020), with a larger increase among females and younger populations than among males and older populations.

span.label: outcome: change in logit prevalence of each disorder, pre-pandemic versus mid-pandemic
span.quote: First, we conducted a systematic literature review to assemble data from surveys measuring the effect of COVID-19 on the prevalence of depressive and anxiety disorders. Second, we used these data in a meta-analysis to (1) estimate the change in prevalence of major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders before versus during the COVID-19 pandemic, (2) predict (through the use of selected indicators of COVID-19 impact) the resulting change in prevalence of each disorder across all GBD locations, and (3) translate changes in prevalence to corresponding changes in burden estimates as years lived with disability (YLDs) and DALYs.

span.label: predictors: a single composite COVID-19 impact indicator, age, sex, and bias covariates for sampling strategy and instrument type
span.quote: Briefly, potential bias covariates that were identified were cross-sectional comparisons informed by random samples, longitudinal comparisons informed by market research and quota samples, cross-sectional comparisons informed by market research and quota samples, and estimates representing combined symptoms of depressive and anxiety disorders
